finding.claim: The caller identity is taken straight from the client-supplied header X-Session-User-Verified, and nothing in this code authenticates it. A client who can reach the app without a gateway that strips and re-sets this header can send any grantee's name and pass every ACL check. This allows deleting and renaming other users' files. Exploitability depends on the deployment: the header name suggests an upstream proxy sets it, but no code in this repo enforces that.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, set by any client that can reach the app
finding.sink: is_allowed/ensure_allowed in acl.py:5 and the protected operations del STORE[fid] (views.py:18) and f['name'] = ... (views.py:27)

trace.note: before_request sets g.user from the raw request header with no signature, session or token validation
ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') compares the spoofed name against resource['grants']
The check is only `action in grants.get(user, [])`, so a spoofed name that has a grant passes
The rename route uses the same spoofed g.user

finding.guards_checked: Searched the only two files in the repo (acl.py and views.py). There is no authentication middleware, no signature check on the header, and no code that strips the header from inbound requests. If an upstream proxy overwrites the header and the app is not directly reachable, this is not exploitable. That deployment detail cannot be verified from this code.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts 403) and is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, result tested at views.py:25). Both work correctly but only compare the unauthenticated header value. No in-repo header stripping or authentication.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 trusts the raw X-Session-User-Verified header and acl.py:5 only checks that name against grants, so the app does nothing to stop spoofing. Whether a gateway overwrites the header, which is what the "Verified" name suggests, cannot be determined from these two files.
